learningObjective: Compare AOT artifact deployment (all lowering done ahead of first invocation) with JIT compilation (lowering triggered on the first suitable call), and identify the trade-offs.
stem: Which statement most accurately contrasts an Ahead-of-Time (AOT) artifact (e.g., AOTInductor .so, TensorRT plan) with a JIT-compiled workflow (e.g., default torch.compile)?

options.text: JIT is always faster than AOT at steady state because JIT observes real inputs and re-optimizes on every call; AOT compiles once and cannot adapt, so its steady-state performance is capped below any JIT implementation.

AOT and JIT produce identical binaries; the only difference is the file extension, and either mode can be selected transparently at inference time without any change to compilation semantics or shape support.

The AOT artifact avoids first-call compilation latency and can be shipped independently of the compiler, but generally requires known shapes/dtypes at build time; JIT compiles lazily on first call, absorbing warmup cost in exchange for shape/dtype flexibility.

AOT requires the source model be present at run time; the compiler is re-invoked from the artifact each time the runtime restarts, which is what enables cross-target dispatch on ARM and x86 from a single file.

explanation: AOT compilation lowers the model to a deployable artifact (shared library, plan file, VM executable) before deployment. The runtime then loads that artifact directly — no compiler needed, no first-call warmup — but the artifact is specialized to the shape/dtype/hardware assumptions used at build time. JIT trades first-call latency and a compiler dependency at run time for the ability to specialize to real observed inputs (dynamic shapes, guards). Neither strictly dominates the other at steady state.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: at steady state, an AOT-compiled artifact typically matches or beats JIT because it has already paid the compilation cost; JIT does not re-optimize per call.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: AOT and JIT differ in when compilation happens and what assumptions the artifact encodes.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: describes the standard AOT vs JIT trade-off (compile-time vs run-time specialization).
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: an AOT artifact does not require the source model or the compiler at run time — that's the point of AOT.

assumptions: Both AOT and JIT stacks emit the same underlying kernels (Triton, cuBLAS, etc.) so we are comparing compilation phase, not code quality.
nonImplications: Does not imply that JIT is always slower to first-response; systems can cache JIT artifacts across process starts.
Does not imply AOT is impossible with dynamic shapes; some AOT stacks (AOTInductor with dynamic dims, TensorRT with optimization profiles) support ranges.

distractorRationales.A: Confuses JIT observation with per-call re-optimization.
